title: The Confessions, Rousseau
subject: litterature
description: Rousseau tells his own life with an honesty nobody had risked before. The Confessions invent modern autobiography and open the way to Romanticism.

hero.hook: “I have resolved on an enterprise which has no precedent”: that is how modern autobiography begins.

blocks.text: The **Confessions** of **Jean-Jacques Rousseau**, published after his death between **1782** and **1789**, mark the birth of modern autobiography. Rousseau tells his own life. The self becomes an object of literary investigation, not just a pretext for talking about History.

Rousseau breaks with aristocratic memoirs, the accounts great men wrote to glorify their deeds, and with religious confession, the avowal made to God. He is after self-understanding, not forgiveness. The book covers his childhood in Geneva, his years of wandering and his career as a writer and philosopher.

“I have resolved on an enterprise which has no precedent”: with that sentence Rousseau defines the **[[autobiographical pact]]**, the author's promise to tell the truth about himself, a notion theorized later by Philippe Lejeune. He tells his life for its own sake, not to glorify History through it.

blocks.caption: Jean-Jacques Rousseau: radical sincerity and solitude

blocks.text: Rousseau was so anxious about the safety of his manuscript that he often traveled with the pages of the Confessions pressed against him in a canvas bag.

Unlike the **Confessions of Saint Augustine**, the Christian model of avowal from the 4th century, the judge here is no longer God but the reader. Rousseau makes confession secular and turns authenticity into the supreme value. Truth lies in being faithful to feelings, not only to objective facts.

Rousseau confesses a stolen ribbon, his taste for being spanked by **Mademoiselle Lambercier**, and his relationship with **[[Mme de Warens]]**, the woman who took him in at 16 and became his protector, and whom he called “Maman.” He also admits leaving his five children at the **Enfants-Trouvés**, the Paris foundling hospital.

blocks.caption: Nature in Rousseau: the mirror of a solitary soul

blocks.text: By saying everything bad about himself, he takes from his enemies the power to denounce him. Landscape becomes the mirror of a new sensibility, the ground of **[[Romanticism]]**, the movement that exalts feeling and nature, and of nostalgia for lost time.

Rousseau wrote the second part in exile, his books burned in Paris and Geneva. Convinced that the whole world was plotting against him, he set out to rescue his memory from his critics, **Voltaire** among them.

He presents himself as the man of **[[Rousseauism and the "noble savage"]]**: naturally good, corrupted by a hypocritical society. Rousseau believed that man is good by nature and that society is what spoils him. The reader becomes an accomplice in a passionate defense. Voltaire, in an anonymous pamphlet, had revealed the abandoned children, forcing Rousseau into public confession and into owning his contradictions.

The influence is immense: **Chateaubriand**, **Stendhal**, **George Sand**, **Goethe**, **Tolstoy**. Rousseau anticipates **Freud**, the founder of psychoanalysis, by showing that childhood and sexuality shape the adult.
He makes the individual sacred: every life, however modest, deserves to be told. That democratization of the subject feeds the private diary and, much later, the display of the self on social media.

By daring to say “I” without a heroic mask, Rousseau opens the way to diaries and to first-person novels. Confession becomes a genre in its own right, and personal truth a literary value. Even his contradictions, a champion of childhood who was an absent father, are part of the project: to show a real man, not a model.
The **Confessions** invent modern autobiography by putting psychological sincerity and childhood at the heart of literature, against a society judged to be corrupting.
